nodes.label: Arrays
nodes.description: A contiguous block of memory storing elements of the same type, accessed by index in O(1) time. The most fundamental data structure.

nodes.label: Linked Lists
nodes.description: A sequence of nodes where each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Supports efficient insertion and deletion but lacks random access.

nodes.label: Stacks
nodes.description: A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure supporting push and pop operations. Used in function call management, expression evaluation, and undo systems.

nodes.label: Queues
nodes.description: A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure supporting enqueue and dequeue operations. Used in scheduling, buffering, and breadth-first traversals.

nodes.label: Recursion
nodes.description: A technique where a function calls itself with a smaller input and a base case to terminate. Essential for tree traversals, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking.

nodes.label: Hashing
nodes.description: A technique that maps keys to array indices using a hash function. Enables average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion when collisions are handled properly.

nodes.label: Hash Tables
nodes.description: A data structure that implements an associative array using hashing. Handles collisions via chaining (linked lists) or open addressing (probing).

nodes.label: Trees: Introduction
nodes.description: A hierarchical data structure with a root node and children forming a non-cyclic connected graph. Key terms: root, leaf, parent, child, height, depth.

nodes.label: Binary Trees
nodes.description: A tree where each node has at most two children (left and right). The foundation for BSTs, heaps, and expression trees.

nodes.label: Tree Traversals
nodes.description: Methods to visit every node in a tree: inorder (left-root-right), preorder (root-left-right), postorder (left-right-root), and level-order (BFS). Each produces a different ordering.

nodes.label: Binary Search Trees
nodes.description: A binary tree where the left subtree contains only nodes with keys less than the parent, and the right subtree only greater. Supports O(log n) average search, insert, delete.

nodes.label: Balanced BSTs (AVL / Red-Black)
nodes.description: Self-balancing binary search trees that maintain O(log n) height through rotations. AVL trees enforce strict balance; red-black trees use color properties.

nodes.label: Heaps & Priority Queues
nodes.description: A complete binary tree satisfying the heap property (max-heap: parent ≥ children, min-heap: parent ≤ children). Efficiently supports extract-min/max in O(log n). Typically stored as an array.

nodes.label: Basic Sorting (Bubble, Selection, Insertion)
nodes.description: Simple comparison-based sorting algorithms running in O(n²) worst case. Useful for understanding sorting fundamentals: comparisons, swaps, stability, and in-place operation.

nodes.label: Advanced Sorting (Merge Sort, Quick Sort)
nodes.description: Divide-and-conquer sorting algorithms. Merge sort is O(n log n) guaranteed and stable. Quick sort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case, typically faster in practice.

nodes.label: Graphs: Introduction
nodes.description: A set of vertices connected by edges. Can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Represented via adjacency matrix or adjacency list.

nodes.label: Graph Traversals (BFS & DFS)
nodes.description: Breadth-First Search (BFS) uses a queue to explore level by level. Depth-First Search (DFS) uses a stack/recursion to explore as deep as possible before backtracking.

nodes.label: Shortest Path Algorithms
nodes.description: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in weighted graphs with non-negative edges. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights. Both build on graph traversal foundations.

nodes.label: Tries (Prefix Trees)
nodes.description: A tree-like data structure where each node represents a character. Used for efficient prefix-based search, autocomplete, and dictionary storage. Lookup is O(key length).

nodes.label: Dynamic Programming
nodes.description: An optimization technique that solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results (memoization or tabulation) to avoid redundant computation.
